paragraphs: When a prompt describes several objects, a text-to-image model can give some objects more attention than others. This paper investigates how that imbalance originates in the text encoder, which converts the prompt into representations used for image generation. Its analysis connects the encoder’s causal processing with information loss and a preference for the first object mentioned.

The authors examine how these text representations affect the resulting images, then propose an optimization that balances the information they carry. The method requires no training. In Stable Diffusion, they report a 125.42% improvement in information balance. This result concerns the stated balance measure, rather than a general percentage improvement in image quality.

The paper also introduces an automatic measure of whether requested objects appear and are represented accurately. It reports 81% agreement with human assessments and more accurate measurement of information loss than existing methods. Together, these contributions identify text representations as a practical intervention point and make object-level failures more directly measurable than overall text-image similarity alone.
neurips-2024-a-cat-is-a-cat-not-a-dog-un.tldr: A training-free adjustment to text embeddings improves object information balance, while a new metric measures object omissions and inaccuracies.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning builds molecular representations by learning which examples should be treated as similar or different. Conventional molecular graph modifications, such as masking nodes or removing subgraphs, can create misleading training pairs. A pair labeled similar may be a false positive, while a pair labeled different may be a false negative, weakening the resulting representations.

This paper proposes a probability-based framework that learns how much weight to give these pairs. Bayesian modeling supplies a learnable distribution over weights, allowing the method to identify and reduce the influence of misleading comparisons. Training uses stochastic expectation-maximization: it alternates between refining probability estimates for sample weights and updating the representation model.

The method outperforms existing approaches on 13 of 15 MoleculeNet property-prediction benchmarks and 8 of 12 QM9 benchmarks, with reported state-of-the-art average results. These findings support adapting the training signal to uncertainty in the pairs themselves. The contribution is therefore a way to make molecular contrastive learning less dependent on the reliability of conventional graph augmentations.
neurips-2024-a-probability-contrastive-l.tldr: Learning probabilistic weights for misleading molecular pairs improves contrastive representations and property-prediction results.

paragraphs: Public speech datasets can be difficult to use together because finding, accessing, and integrating them requires substantial effort. BIGOS V2 addresses that practical obstacle to evaluating automatic speech recognition. The researchers build a system for surveying available datasets, organizing them into a catalog, and curating them for reproducible comparisons of speech recognition systems.

They apply the system to Polish, curating more than 24 datasets and evaluating 25 models. The resulting benchmark contains 600 combinations of systems, models, and test sets across eight analysis scenarios. The authors describe it as the most extensive Polish comparison of commercial and free speech recognition systems available at the time of the work.

The contribution includes public curated datasets and benchmark results, alongside open-source evaluation tools. This makes the evaluation process itself available for reuse and community improvement. It also provides a basis for adapting the approach to other languages. The paper’s central value is a broader, reproducible evaluation resource that makes existing speech data more usable.
neurips-2024-bigos-v2-benchmark-for-poli.tldr: BIGOS V2 organizes public speech datasets and open tools into a large, reproducible benchmark for Polish speech recognition.

paragraphs: Testing graph algorithms can require collections whose graphs differ substantially in structure. This paper treats the construction of such collections as an explicit optimization problem. Its starting point is that structural diversity needs a definition: choosing how to measure differences between graphs also determines what kinds of variation a generator will be encouraged to produce.

The authors discuss how to select a suitable diversity measure, then compare several ways to optimize it. These include standard random graph models, local changes to graphs, genetic algorithms, and neural generative models. Their comparisons show that deliberately optimizing diversity can produce substantially more diverse collections than basic random graph generators under the measures considered.

The generated collections also reveal properties of the measures themselves. Optimizing different diversity measures can yield graphs with very different structures, exposing which distinctions the underlying graph distances emphasize. The work therefore offers both methods for building varied test collections and a way to examine whether a chosen notion of diversity captures the structural differences of interest.
neurips-2024-challenges-of-generating-st.tldr: Explicitly optimizing graph diversity improves on basic random generators and reveals how diversity measures favor different structures.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models can be adapted to follow instructions through additional training, but learning successive tasks raises a retention problem. CoIN examines how these models behave during continual instruction tuning. Its benchmark contains ten datasets covering eight tasks, allowing evaluation of factors including task order, instruction diversity, and the amount of instruction data.

The authors supplement conventional evaluation with an LLM-based metric intended to assess how much knowledge remains available for reasoning. This distinction matters because poor performance on an earlier task can reflect different failures: a model may lose relevant knowledge, or it may retain knowledge while becoming worse at following that task’s instructions.

Evaluations of several models find catastrophic forgetting, with failures of instruction alignment identified as the main contributor rather than loss of reasoning knowledge. The authors introduce MoELoRA and report that it effectively preserves earlier instruction alignment. The findings direct attention toward retaining how models respond to instructions when diagnosing and addressing deterioration during continued training.
neurips-2024-coin-a-benchmark-of-continu.tldr: CoIN finds that continual multimodal instruction tuning mainly forgets instruction alignment and introduces MoELoRA to help retain it.

paragraphs: Deep equilibrium models can achieve strong performance with relatively few parameters, but their iterative inference can require substantial computation. DeltaDEQ investigates a useful unevenness in those iterations: some dimensions of the model’s state settle much earlier than others. The authors call this heterogeneous convergence and also observe it in other iterative methods.

The proposed method stores previous results of linear operations, including fully connected and convolutional layers. It propagates a state activation only when its change exceeds a threshold. Dimensions that have already settled can therefore avoid repeated computation, concentrating updates on the parts of the state that are still changing meaningfully.

The authors report reductions in floating-point operations of 84% for an implicit neural representation task, 73% on Sintel, and 76% on KITTI for optical flow estimation. Task accuracy remains comparable to models that update the full state. These results show how exploiting uneven convergence can substantially reduce arithmetic work without requiring all state dimensions to finish converging together.
neurips-2024-deltadeq-exploiting-heterog.tldr: DeltaDEQ skips updates to already settled state dimensions, substantially reducing computation while preserving comparable accuracy in tested tasks.

paragraphs: Code-generation benchmarks can become less informative when their examples leak into training data or when aggregate scores conceal differences between programming domains. EvoCodeBench addresses both concerns through planned periodic updates and explicit domain labels. Its first release contains 275 samples from 25 repositories, collected through a rigorous pipeline designed to reflect real-world repository characteristics.

The benchmark defines ten programming domains and evaluates models using both Pass@k and Domain-Specific Improvement. These measurements identify domains where particular models are relatively comfortable or struggle. The evolving collection is intended to avoid leakage, while the domain breakdown helps practitioners assess models against the kinds of programming work they actually need.

Across eight evaluated models, the reported highest GPT-4 Pass@1 is 20.74%. GPT-4 leads in most domains but trails others in the Internet domain; StarCoder 2-15B performs especially well in Database, exceeding even 33B models. These findings show why overall rankings can be insufficient for model selection. The benchmark, prompts, and completions are released for further analysis.
neurips-2024-evocodebench-an-evolving-co.tldr: EvoCodeBench combines evolving repository tasks with domain-specific evaluations that expose differences hidden by overall code-generation scores.

paragraphs: Time series can change alongside social events described in news, including unexpected incidents and shifts in behavior. This paper develops a forecasting approach that reasons across numerical sequences and news text. Language provides the common medium for connecting descriptions of events with fluctuations in the series, adding contextual information to the forecasting process.

LLM-based agents repeatedly filter irrelevant news and evaluate predictions through a reasoning process. That feedback refines both the logic used to select news and the robustness of the agents’ output. The selected events are then combined with time series data to fine-tune a pretrained language model, which forecasts the numerical sequence as digits.

The authors report significant improvements in forecasting accuracy from this approach. The findings support the usefulness of selecting and interpreting unstructured news before incorporating it into numerical prediction. Reflection is central to the design because the relevance of an event is revisited as predictions are assessed, allowing the news-selection process to improve alongside the forecasting workflow.
neurips-2024-from-news-to-forecast-integ.tldr: LLM agents refine news selection through reflection, helping a fine-tuned language model produce more accurate time-series forecasts.

paragraphs: A simple bilevel problem has two linked objectives: first identify solutions that optimize a lower-level function, then minimize an upper-level function within that solution set. This paper studies the case where both functions are convex. Even with that structure, the requirement to optimize over another problem’s optimal solutions creates a fundamental computational difficulty.

The authors show that a particular class of methods, first-order zero-respecting algorithms, cannot obtain the approximate optimal value of these problems. They therefore pursue the weaker approximate-solution target considered in recent work. Their method reformulates the bilevel task as a functionally constrained problem, providing a different route to that attainable approximation goal.

The resulting algorithm achieves near-optimal rates for both smooth and nonsmooth problems. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first near-optimal method covering these cases under standard smoothness or Lipschitz-continuity assumptions. The positive result concerns weak approximate solutions, so it fits alongside the impossibility result without claiming to overcome that stronger computational barrier.
neurips-2024-functionally-constrained-al.tldr: A constrained reformulation yields near-optimal weak approximation rates for convex bilevel problems despite a stronger approximation barrier.

paragraphs: Creating an animatable head avatar from one image requires recovering facial appearance while supporting changes in expression. GAGA addresses this task using a representation built from 3D Gaussians. The motivation is practical: existing approaches based on neural radiance fields can incur heavy rendering costs and make facial reenactment too slow for real-time use.

GAGA predicts the Gaussian parameters from the input image in a single forward pass. Its central dual-lifting method produces Gaussians intended to preserve identity and facial detail. Global image features and a 3D morphable model provide additional information for constructing the Gaussians used to control expressions, connecting appearance reconstruction with the ability to animate the face.

After training, the model can reconstruct previously unseen identities without optimization specific to each person and render reenactments in real time. Experiments report better reconstruction quality and expression accuracy than previous methods. These findings indicate that the proposed representation and prediction process can support both detailed reconstruction and efficient animation within the evaluated setting.
neurips-2024-generalizable-and-animatabl.tldr: GAGA creates animatable Gaussian head avatars from one image and supports real-time reenactment without person-specific optimization.

paragraphs: When several machine-learning services serve different users, users may select whichever service minimizes their personal loss. The services then adapt using those interactions. This creates coupled learning dynamics whose eventual outcomes depend strongly on initialization. Finding a good starting point is difficult because preferences are initially unknown and the total loss landscape can contain poor local minima.

The paper proposes a randomized algorithm that adaptively chooses a minimal set of users from whom to collect data. It uses those observations to initialize the services, addressing the problem of limited feedback before deployment. The aim is to obtain useful starting conditions without first acquiring complete preference information for every user.

Under mild assumptions on the loss functions, the initialization achieves total loss within a factor of the global optimum achievable with complete preference data. That factor grows logarithmically with the number of services. The result extends the k-means++ guarantee to a broader problem class, with experiments on real and semi-synthetic datasets complementing the theory.
neurips-2024-initializing-services-in-in.tldr: Adaptive sampling of users gives multiple learning services an initialization with a logarithmic approximation guarantee under stated loss assumptions.

paragraphs: Remote-sensing images can be scarce and difficult to annotate, making adaptation of pretrained models attractive. Unequal class frequencies introduce another problem: features associated with common classes can dominate those of rare classes. This paper proposes debLoRA, a training approach designed to reduce that imbalance when adapting models with LoRA and its variants.

The method uses unsupervised clustering to identify attributes shared by common and rare classes. It then uses those shared attributes to diversify the representations of rare classes. This focuses the intervention on learned features, aiming to improve minority-class representation while preserving the useful information already available for classes with more examples.

Experiments cover transfer from natural images to optical remote-sensing images and from optical to multispectrum remote-sensing images. Classification and oriented detection are evaluated on DOTA and FUSRS. The authors report consistent improvements over prior methods, including tail-class gains of up to 3.3 and 4.7 percentage points in the respective transfer settings, while maintaining performance on common classes.
neurips-2024-learning-de-biased-represen.tldr: debLoRA uses clustered shared attributes to improve rare-class representations during remote-sensing adaptation while preserving common-class performance.

paragraphs: Score-based diffusion models rely on score matching during training, but the objective includes an expensive Jacobian-trace computation. Existing ways to avoid that calculation have their own drawbacks, including training instability and formulations that learn a denoising vector field as an approximation to a true score. This paper develops another way to remove that computational obstacle.

The proposed method, local curvature smoothing with Stein’s identity, uses Stein’s identity to bypass the Jacobian trace. The authors present this reformulation as providing both efficient computation and effective regularization. Its significance lies in changing the training objective’s computational treatment while retaining a score-matching approach to learning the model.

The reported evaluations show better sample generation than existing methods and performance comparable to widely used denoising score matching on FID, Inception score, and bits per dimension. The authors also demonstrate realistic images at 1024 by 1024 resolution. Together, these results support LCSS as a practical alternative for score-based generation, including at the demonstrated high resolution.
neurips-2024-local-curvature-smoothing-w.tldr: LCSS uses Stein’s identity to avoid an expensive score-matching computation while achieving competitive image-generation performance.

paragraphs: Future motion can have several plausible outcomes, and those possibilities need not be symmetrically distributed. This paper argues that a normalizing-flow trajectory predictor starting from a standard Gaussian can struggle to express that diversity. The authors attribute the problem to a mismatch involving the symmetric, single-mode starting distribution, multimodal outcomes, and the supervision losses.

Mixed Gaussian Flow replaces that starting distribution with a mixture of Gaussians. The mixture is constructed by analyzing trajectory patterns already present in the training examples, so it requires no additional annotations. Its multiple modes and asymmetry provide a more expressive basis for representing the different futures that the predictor should consider.

The authors report that this change improves both diversity and control over probabilistic trajectory generation. On UCY/ETH and SDD, MGF achieves reported state-of-the-art results for trajectory alignment and diversity. The findings support changing the prior as a way to improve the range of predicted futures while also maintaining strong agreement with the trajectories used for evaluation.
neurips-2024-mgf-mixed-gaussian-flow-for.tldr: MGF learns a mixed Gaussian prior from trajectory patterns to improve the diversity, alignment, and controllability of predicted motion.

paragraphs: Diffusion methods can generate motion through iterative refinement, but approaches learned from data may not use available information about a system’s dynamics. That can restrict transfer to new scenarios, such as robots with different dynamics. Model-Based Diffusion approaches trajectory optimization by using the problem’s model information directly and does not require external training data.

Its central step is to compute the score function explicitly from information in the trajectory-optimization problem. This supplies the guidance for the diffusion process. The authors also connect the method to sampling-based optimization. Although external data are unnecessary, demonstrations or other data can still be incorporated to steer the process, including data of varying quality.

Evaluations on challenging contact-rich tasks show MBD outperforming state-of-the-art reinforcement-learning and sampling-based trajectory-optimization methods. The method can also use imperfect or infeasible data, including partial-state demonstrations for high-dimensional humanoids. These findings show how model information and optional demonstrations can be combined within diffusion-based optimization, extending its practical use beyond dependence on a suitable training collection.
neurips-2024-model-based-diffusion-for-t.tldr: Model-Based Diffusion solves trajectory-optimization problems using explicit model information, with optional guidance from even imperfect demonstrations.

paragraphs: This paper studies online decisions intended to benefit multiple agents fairly, using Nash social welfare: the geometric mean of their rewards. Earlier related bandit work instead used their reward product. The distinction changes the learning guarantees, motivating an analysis of whether accumulated regret can grow slower than the number of decision rounds.

For stochastic bandits with N agents and K arms, the authors obtain regret of order K^(2/N) T^((N−1)/N), up to logarithmic factors. They prove the dependence on T is tight. This contrasts with the square-root dependence previously obtained for the product objective. With adversarial rewards and bandit feedback, they prove that sublinear regret is impossible.

Full-information feedback permits two algorithms with square-root regret. One has no dependence on the number of agents and extends to a broad class of welfare functions; the other improves dependence on the number of arms and is preferable with few agents. They also establish logarithmic regret when an agent is indifferent between arms, highlighting how feedback and reward structure affect attainable fairness guarantees.
neurips-2024-no-regret-learning-for-fair.tldr: The paper establishes achievable and impossible regret guarantees for Nash social welfare across stochastic, adversarial, and full-information settings.

paragraphs: M-natural-concave functions, also called gross substitute valuations, arise in discrete mathematics and economics. This paper studies how to maximize them when their values are initially unknown and must be learned through interaction. It separates settings with stochastic noisy observations from adversarial settings, asking what learning guarantees are computationally achievable in each.

With T queries to an unbiased noisy value oracle, the authors provide stochastic-bandit algorithms with simple regret of order T^(-1/2) and cumulative regret of order T^(2/3). These address the quality of a recommended solution and losses accumulated during learning, respectively. A key technical result shows that greedy maximization remains robust to local errors, supporting optimization from imperfect feedback.

The adversarial result draws a different boundary. Unless P equals NP, no algorithm running in polynomial time per round can guarantee regret of order T^(1−c) for any fixed positive c, even with full-information feedback. The proof reduces a three-matroid intersection problem to this setting, showing that richer feedback alone does not remove the stated computational barrier.
neurips-2024-no-regret-m-natural-concave.tldr: Stochastic noisy feedback permits provable learning for M-natural-concave maximization, while adversarial learning faces a conditional polynomial-time barrier.

paragraphs: Capture the Flag challenges provide cybersecurity problems that can be used to examine how language models reason and act through a task. NYU CTF Bench builds a scalable, open-source collection of challenges from popular competitions. The collection includes metadata intended to support model testing and adaptive learning, creating a specialized resource for evaluating these capabilities.

The authors pair the dataset with a fully automated evaluation framework. It uses language-model function calling and supports external tools, allowing evaluation of workflows that involve actions as well as textual responses. They assess five language models spanning black-box and open-source systems, and compare model performance with human performance.

The work provides infrastructure for studying interactive cybersecurity and automated task planning. Its dataset and framework make it possible to develop, test, and refine approaches within a shared challenge setting. The comparisons offer insights into potential cybersecurity applications, while the stated contribution centers on establishing an evaluation platform and a foundation for further research into model effectiveness.
neurips-2024-nyu-ctf-bench-a-scalable-op.tldr: NYU CTF Bench combines open cybersecurity challenges with an automated tool-using framework for evaluating language models.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents can receive intrinsic rewards for visiting novel states, but the usefulness of those rewards depends on how novelty is measured. This paper examines bonuses based on differences between adjacent states. It identifies scalability problems in methods requiring episodic count-based scaling and approximation problems in methods based on bisimulation metrics, particularly for difficult exploration tasks.

Effective Metric-based Exploration-bonus, or EME, introduces a state-discrepancy metric supported by theoretical analysis. It also adjusts the bonus using a diversity-enhanced scaling factor based on the variance of predictions from an ensemble of reward models. This combines a revised measure of state difference with an adaptive way of determining how strongly that difference should encourage exploration.

Experiments cover hard exploration tasks in Atari, Minigrid, Robosuite, and Habitat. The authors report that the results demonstrate scalability across these scenarios. The approach emphasizes two linked design choices: defining a meaningful difference between states and scaling its exploratory value dynamically, both of which influence how effectively an agent seeks new experience.
neurips-2024-rethinking-exploration-in-r.tldr: EME combines a theoretically supported state-discrepancy metric with adaptive reward-ensemble scaling to improve exploration in challenging tasks.

paragraphs: Vision-language models answer questions about images, making the integrity of their training data relevant to the reliability of everyday responses. Shadowcast examines how poisoned training examples can redirect those responses. Its poisoned samples are described as visually indistinguishable from benign images with matching text, making the manipulation difficult to recognize from appearance alone.

The paper studies two forms of manipulation. Label attacks cause incorrect object or identity labels, while persuasion attacks exploit text generation to produce seemingly reasoned misinformation. In the reported experiments, the attack achieves its intended effects with as few as 50 poisoned samples. This extends the concern beyond isolated naming mistakes to persuasive explanations that support false claims.

The authors also report transfer across different model architectures and continued effectiveness under varied prompts, training-data augmentation, and image compression. These findings make the attack relevant to black-box settings and the tested processing conditions. The broader implication is that ordinary users can receive deceptive responses from compromised models even when their own prompts are benign.
neurips-2024-shadowcast-stealthy-data-po.tldr: Shadowcast shows that small amounts of stealthy poisoned data can induce misidentification and persuasive misinformation in vision-language models.

paragraphs: The Multimodal Universe is a collection of astronomical observations assembled specifically for machine-learning research. It brings together hundreds of millions of observations totaling 100 TB. The contribution is a scientific data resource at a scale intended to support the development of large multimodal models for applications in astronomy and related scientific work.

Its contents span several forms of measurement: multichannel and hyperspectral images, spectra, multivariate time series, and associated scientific measurements and metadata. This variety is central to the project’s purpose. Researchers are given a collection covering multiple kinds of astronomical information, providing material for studying models that work with different observational representations.

The dataset is accompanied by benchmark tasks reflecting standard machine-learning practices in astrophysics. These tasks give the resource an evaluation component as well as a training-data role. The authors also provide the code used to compile the collection and instructions for accessing it, supporting reuse of both the assembled observations and the process behind their compilation.
neurips-2024-the-multimodal-universe-ena.tldr: The Multimodal Universe assembles 100 TB of varied astronomical observations and benchmark tasks for large-scale scientific machine learning.

paragraphs: Training a classifier to resist adversarial perturbations involves more than selecting a robust training objective. This paper examines implicit bias: the preferences introduced by the optimization process and model architecture. It asks how those preferences affect robust generalization, connecting choices made during training with robustness beyond the examples used to fit the model.

The theoretical investigation focuses on linear classification under adversarial perturbations. For a given set of allowed perturbations, the authors study what regularization would ideally improve generalization, including robust generalization. They then show that implicit bias in robust empirical risk minimization can significantly affect robustness through either the optimization algorithm or the architecture.

Synthetic-data simulations verify the paper’s predictions, and experiments with deep neural networks investigate the importance of the same issue in richer models. The contribution is a connection between the perturbations a model should resist and the preferences its training process imposes. It establishes optimizer and architecture choices as consequential parts of studying robust generalization.
neurips-2024-the-price-of-implicit-bias-.tldr: Optimization algorithms and architectures impose implicit preferences that can significantly affect adversarially robust generalization.

paragraphs: Uncertainty in a language-model response can have different causes. Epistemic uncertainty reflects missing knowledge about the truth, while aleatoric uncertainty can arise because several answers are possible. This paper aims to distinguish these sources so that uncertainty caused by a knowledge gap can be identified even when legitimate answer variation is also present.

The authors derive an information-theoretic metric for detecting high epistemic uncertainty. It can be computed using only model outputs from a special iterative prompting process, in which earlier responses inform later prompts. The approach therefore obtains its signal through repeated interaction with the model and supports analysis of both single-answer and multiple-answer responses.

Experiments demonstrate advantages over standard uncertainty strategies, including response log-likelihood thresholding, which the authors identify as unable to detect hallucinations in the multiple-answer case. The work also explores how iterative prompting can amplify the probability assigned to an output. Its central contribution is a way to separate unreliable knowledge from uncertainty that accompanies a range of possible answers.
neurips-2024-to-believe-or-not-to-believ.tldr: An output-only metric uses iterative prompting to distinguish uncertainty from missing knowledge from uncertainty due to multiple possible answers.

paragraphs: This paper investigates diffusion-model generalization by examining the denoisers learned at different noise levels. The authors observe that these nonlinear denoisers become increasingly linear as models move from memorization toward generalization. They then train linear models to reproduce the denoisers’ mappings, using these simpler counterparts to probe what statistical structure the original models capture.

The fitted linear denoisers approximately match optimal denoisers for a multivariate Gaussian whose mean and covariance come from the training data. The authors interpret this as an inductive bias toward using the dataset’s Gaussian structure, especially covariance information, during generation. The result identifies a statistical tendency within learned denoisers rather than claiming that all their behavior is linear.

Empirically, this tendency is associated with the generalization regime and becomes clearer when model capacity is small relative to dataset size. In highly overparameterized models, it appears early in training before full memorization. These observations connect generalization behavior with model capacity and training progress, offering an explanation for a component of diffusion models’ observed ability to generalize.
neurips-2024-understanding-generalizabil.tldr: Diffusion denoisers show a stronger tendency to capture training-data covariance structure when operating in a generalization regime.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a vision-language model can be undermined by incorrect labels in the target dataset. DeFT addresses this problem by using the image-text alignment learned during large-scale pretraining to identify likely labeling errors. The framework turns that existing relationship between visual and textual features into a tool for selecting cleaner examples during adaptation.

For each class, DeFT learns both a positive and a negative textual prompt. The positive prompt captures distinctive class features, while the negative prompt acts as a learned threshold separating clean examples from noisy ones. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts the visual encoder so its representations align with these prompts, linking sample selection with the model’s adaptation process.

The resulting clean samples are used to fine-tune pretrained models for downstream tasks. Experiments on seven datasets with synthetic and real-world label noise support the framework’s effectiveness in both noisy-label detection and image classification. The findings indicate that pretrained cross-modal alignment can help identify unreliable supervision while also supporting useful adaptation to a new task.
neurips-2024-vision-language-models-are-.tldr: DeFT learns positive and negative class prompts to detect noisy labels and improve vision-language model fine-tuning.
